title: Choosing a Concentration Method with a Trap Board-style
question: A plant has a sulphide ore whose particles can preferentially attach to air bubbles, but it also contains gangue that differs from the ore in density. Which statement is the strongest conclusion?

options.text: Froth flotation and hydraulic washing are synonyms, so the same principle governs both.
Froth flotation is suitable because of the ore’s behaviour with bubbles; hydraulic washing could be considered separately if density differences permit effective separation.
The density difference proves that froth flotation cannot be used for any part of the process.
Magnetic separation must be chosen even when no difference in magnetic behaviour is established.

explanation:
Froth flotation and hydraulic washing rely on different separation principles. The sulphide ore’s ability to attach to bubbles supports flotation, whereas a useful density difference may support hydraulic washing. Neither observation alone establishes that the alternative method is impossible.

title: Diagnosing Multiple Errors in a Hall–Héroult Diagram Board-style
question: A diagram shows alumina dissolved in cryolite and fluorspar at about 950°C. However, the labels show the carbon-lined tank connected to the positive terminal, graphite rods connected to the negative terminal, and aluminium deposited around the rods. Which correction is required?

options.text: Reverse the electrode connections so the tank is the negative cathode and the graphite rods are the positive anodes; aluminium then collects at the bottom.
Keep the electrode connections and collect aluminium at the positive graphite rods.
Connect both electrodes to the positive terminal and collect oxygen at the bottom.
Replace the molten electrolyte with solid bauxite and reverse the direction of ion movement.

explanation:
The carbon-lined steel tank is the negative cathode, and the graphite rods are the positive anodes. Aluminium ions gain electrons at the cathode, and molten aluminium collects at the bottom. Option B retains the incorrect polarity.

title: Choosing the Correct Method from Ore Chemistry Board-style
question: Two concentrated ores are processed separately. Sample P is carbonate calamine, ZnCO₃, while sample Q is sulphide zinc blende, ZnS. Which statement correctly explains their conversion into oxides?

options.text: Both must be roasted in excess air and both release SO₂.
Both must undergo electrolysis because they contain zinc.
P is calcined to release CO₂, while Q is roasted in excess air to produce SO₂.
P is roasted to produce CO₂, while Q is calcined without air to produce SO₂.

explanation:
Carbonate ores undergo calcination:


ZnCO_3xrightarrow{ΔZnO+CO₂}


Sulphide ores undergo roasting:


2ZnS+3O₂→2ZnO+2SO₂


The type of compound, rather than merely the metal it contains, determines the appropriate treatment.

question: During smelting, a technician records a rocky impurity, an intentionally added material and a newly formed waste layer. Which record correctly uses the terms gangue, flux and slag?

Gangue is the metal oxide being reduced; flux is the anode residue; slag is the refined metal.
Gangue is the unwanted material associated with the ore; flux is added to react with suitable gangue; slag is the resulting product.

explanation:
The terms identify three distinct things: naturally associated impurities, an added substance used to react with suitable impurities, and the product formed by that reaction. Interchanging these terms confuses an input with an unwanted constituent and a reaction product.

title: Aluminium Yield from Impure Bauxite: Integrated Calculation
question: A 690 g sample of bauxite ore contains 80% pure Al_2O₃·2H_2O by mass. The remaining 20% is inert gangue. Assuming complete purification, conversion to alumina and electrolytic recovery, what theoretical mass of aluminium can be obtained?
explanation:
First, calculate the mass of pure hydrated bauxite:


m(pure bauxite)=0.80(690)=552 g


Moles of pure bauxite:


n=(552 / 138)=4 mol


One mole of hydrated bauxite yields one mole of alumina. The overall electrolytic equation is:


2Al_2O₃→4Al+3O₂


Therefore, four moles of alumina yield eight moles of aluminium.


m(Al)=8(27)
=216 g


Option A, 408 g, is the mass of alumina theoretically obtained from the purified bauxite; it is not the mass of aluminium.

---

title: Complete Process Audit Board-style
question: A metallurgical plant proposes this order for extracting aluminium: refine bauxite into aluminium hydroxide; directly reduce the hydroxide using carbon; add cryolite after metallic aluminium is formed; then electrolytically refine the aluminium using the same process as extraction. Which correction gives the appropriate route?

options.text: Roast bauxite in excess air to form aluminium metal, use NaOH as the cathode and add cryolite during refining.
Purify bauxite using hot concentrated NaOH; precipitate Al(OH)₃; heat it to Al₂O₃; electrolyse the alumina dissolved in molten cryolite with a little fluorspar; collect aluminium at the cathode.
Electrolyse raw bauxite first; precipitate sodium aluminate from the molten metal; roast aluminium hydroxide to aluminium.
Add graphite to bauxite to produce sodium aluminate, then use cryolite to convert it into pure aluminium without electrolysis.

explanation:
The proper sequence is chemical purification by Baeyer's process, precipitation of aluminium hydroxide, heating to alumina, and electrolytic extraction by the Hall–Héroult process. Aluminium collects at the negative cathode. The proposed route wrongly substitutes carbon reduction for electrolysis and places cryolite after extraction.

title: Limiting Reagent in Baeyer's Process
question: A process vessel contains 276 g of pure bauxite, Al_2O₃·2H_2O, and 120 g of NaOH. Assuming complete reaction of the limiting reagent, calculate the theoretical mass of sodium aluminate, NaAlO₂, formed.
explanation:
The balanced equation is:


Al_2O₃·2H_2O+2NaOH
→
2NaAlO₂+3H_2O


Moles of bauxite:


n=(276 / 138)=2 mol


Moles of NaOH:


n=(120 / 40)=3 mol


Two moles of bauxite require four moles of NaOH, but only three moles are available. Therefore, NaOH is the limiting reagent.

The equation gives a 1:1 mole ratio of NaOH to NaAlO₂:


n(NaAlO₂)=3 mol



m=3[23+27+2(16)]
=3(82)
=246 g


Option A assumes that all the bauxite reacts, ignoring the shortage of NaOH.

---

title: Precipitation of Aluminium Hydroxide
question: A sodium aluminate, NaAlO₂, solution contains 246 g of the compound. On dilution and seeding, complete precipitation occurs according to the Baeyer's process equation. What mass of Al(OH)₃ is formed?
explanation:
The balanced equation is:


NaAlO₂+2H_2O
→
Al(OH)₃+NaOH


Molar masses:


M(NaAlO₂)=82



M(Al(OH)₃)=27+3(16+1)=78


Moles of sodium aluminate:


n=(246 / 82)=3 mol


The molar ratio of NaAlO₂ to Al(OH)₃ is 1:1.


m(Al(OH)₃)=3×78
=234 g


Option A incorrectly treats the conversion as producing only 2 mol of aluminium hydroxide.
